title: The sacrifice of everything
theme: The story opens with a father giving away all he owns for the sake of a reward, and names his son, Naciketas.

words.gram: pres. act. participle, m. nom. sg.
words.context: Śaṅkara: «उशन् कामयमानः» — desiring [the fruit of the rite]
Śaṅkara: ha and vai recall a past event
Śaṅkara: vājaśravas is one famed (śravas) for giving food (vāja), or simply a name

words.role: main verb of the first sentence
main verb of the second sentence
words.context: Raṅgarāmānuja explains the perfect āsa (rather than babhūva) as Vedic usage

sandhi.rule: The final n of the participle stands unchanged before h; the base writes the two words without a space.
After ā the visarga is dropped before a voiced sound: P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि) and P. 8.3.22 (हलि सर्वेषाम्).

sandhi.type: aḥ before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: The visarga of aḥ becomes y before a vowel, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), and is then dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य); the hiatus stays.

samasa.meaning: all (his) wealth; vedas here means property, not the Veda

morphology.note: Present active participle of vaś, ‘to wish’, with the weak grade (u for va): Raṅgarāmānuja derives it from vaś with samprasāraṇa. It tells why the father gives: he wants the reward of the rite.

Perfect of as, ‘to be’. Classical Sanskrit uses babhūva; the Veda keeps āsa (Raṅgarāmānuja: in the Veda the perfect may count as sārvadhātuka, P. 3.4.117 (छन्दस्युभयथा), so as is not replaced by bhū).

translation.literal: Desiring [a reward], indeed, the son of Vājaśravas gave all [his] possessions. He had, indeed, a son named Naciketas.
translation.readable: Once, hoping for heaven, the son of Vājaśravas gave away everything he owned. He had a son called Naciketas.

anvaya: उशन् ह वै वाजश्रवसः सर्ववेदसम् ददौ । तस्य ह नचिकेताः नाम पुत्रः आस ॥
syntax: Two short narrative sentences in the perfect tense, the tense of story. The participle uśan (‘desiring’) gives the motive before the verb; the object of desire is left unsaid. The second sentence introduces Naciketas as the son, the person on whom the story will turn.

ambiguities.note: The name means ‘son of Vājaśravas’; Śaṅkara allows that it is either a patronymic from a man famed for giving food or simply a name («रूढितो वा»). Later the father is called Gautama (1.1.10) and Auddālaki Āruṇi (1.1.11); Madhva’s cited verse calls him Uddālaka. How these names relate is a question the text does not settle.
The first mantra is prose, in the style of a brāhmaṇa narrative, though its first line happens to count sixteen syllables.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Narrative prose in two sentences (16 and 13 syllables as written). The Kaṭha’s verses begin with 1.1.3.

beginner: The story begins with a sacrifice. A man known as the son of Vājaśravas performs a great ritual in which the sacrificer gives away all he owns, hoping to win heaven in return. In one sentence the Upaniṣad tells us what he did and why: he wanted the reward. In the next sentence it names his son, Naciketas, still a boy. Nothing yet has been said about death, the self or liberation. The commentators note that the story is told to honour the knowledge that will come: a dramatic frame helps the listener care about the teaching. The father’s motive matters, because the whole Upaniṣad will contrast what we give in order to gain something with what cannot be gained by giving at all.
analogy: Like a story that begins with a rich man emptying his house for a prize, and only then mentions, almost in passing, the child who will become its hero.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: A man called Vājaśravasa, wanting [a reward], gave away all he had; he had a son named Naciketas. The motive (uśan, ‘desiring’) is stated, its object is not.

commentary.q: Why does an Upaniṣad about the self begin with a story?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara’s first sentence on the mantra: «तत्राख्यायिका विद्यास्तुत्यर्था» — the story is there to praise the knowledge. In his introduction he defines the word upaniṣad itself: it is primarily the knowledge, and only secondarily the book — «उपनिषच्छब्देन च व्याचिख्यासितग्रन्थप्रतिपाद्यवेद्यवस्तुविषया विद्या उच्यते», because that knowledge loosens and destroys the seed of transmigration in those who devote themselves to it.

commentary.q: What rite was it, and what did he want?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara names the rite: the Viśvajit, a sacrifice in which all is given away — «विश्वजिता सर्वमेधेनेजे तत्फलं कामयमानः», he sacrificed with the Viśvajit, the all-giving, wanting its fruit. Raṅgarāmānuja draws a consequence from the word uśan: because the rite was performed for a desired result, the correctness of its gifts mattered — «उशन् इत्यनेन कर्मणः काम्यत्वात् दक्षिणासाद्गुण्यम् आवश्यकमिति सूच्यते». That prepares the boy’s objection in the next mantras.

commentary.q: What does the Dvaita tradition add?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Madhva’s bhāṣya opens with verses he cites from other works. One names the father and his aim: «उद्दालकः स्वर्गलोकं ददौ गाश्च निरिन्द्रियाः» — Uddālaka, wanting heaven, gave away even cows that were past use. (The verse is reported as cited by Madhva.)

advaita.text: The narrative serves the teaching: «तत्राख्यायिका विद्यास्तुत्यर्था». The Upaniṣad is the knowledge of Brahman that is one’s inner self, and the book is called upaniṣad only secondarily: «तस्माद्विद्यायां मुख्यया वृत्त्या उपनिषच्छब्दो वर्तते».

visistadvaita.text: Raṅgarāmānuja reads the scene ritually and closely: the sacrifice is a desire-prompted (kāmya) rite, so the adequacy of its gifts is essential — «कर्मणः काम्यत्वात् दक्षिणासाद्गुण्यम् आवश्यकमिति सूच्यते».

dvaita.text: The father is Uddālaka, who gave all for the sake of heaven: «इच्छन् वाजश्रवोनप्ता ददौ सर्वस्वदक्षिणाम्». In the same place Madhva cites a Brahmasāra verse that reads the whole Naciketas teaching as meditation on Viṣṇu in the fire.

schools.disagreement: At this point the schools differ only in emphasis: Śaṅkara on the story as praise of knowledge, Raṅgarāmānuja on the ritual logic of the gift, Madhva (through the verses he cites) on Uddālaka’s wish for heaven.

contemporary.text: A man gives away everything — but in order to receive something greater. Generosity calculated for a return is still a transaction, and the story will soon test whether what he gives is really worth giving. This is a modern reflection, not the text’s claim.

reflect.beginner: When have you given something mainly for what you hoped to get back?
reflect.deeper: Can a gift made for a reward still be a gift? What would distinguish it from a purchase?
reflect.practice: Notice one act of giving today, however small, and ask honestly what you wanted from it.

references.text: The Naciketas story also appears in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (3.11.8); Madhva’s sub-commentator Vedeśatīrtha quotes a Kāṭhaka prose version under 1.1.4. That brāhmaṇa passage is not among this edition’s sources and is not quoted here.
